findings.title: Gerald Voss and his industry-custom testimony appear nowhere in the supplied record
findings.explanation: C-027 fails any answer that lacks a motion in limine to exclude Gerald Voss's industry-custom testimony on MAPC enforcement. C-008 grades how the solver handles that motion's parol-evidence weakness. A full-text search of all 11 documents finds no Voss, no Gerald, no custom or trade-usage expert, no parol-evidence dispute, and no defense witness list. The solver cannot know this witness exists. Every competent answer built from the record therefore fails C-027 and cannot satisfy C-008. Under all-pass scoring, this alone zeroes every run.

findings.suggested_fix: Either add a document (for example a defense expert disclosure or the defendant's witness list naming Voss and his opinions), or delete C-027 and C-008.

findings.title: C-007 requires opposing a Corbin FRE 407 motion about the Findlay memo that the record never mentions
findings.explanation: C-007 fails any answer that does not oppose Corbin Supply's motion in limine to exclude the Findlay memo under FRE 407. No document mentions such a motion, Rule 407, or remedial measures. The pretrial order asks each party to state its position on the opponent's motions only 'to the extent such positions are known.' A competent drafter could address the memo's admissibility in general (for example, as a party-opponent statement), but would have no reason to rebut a Rule 407 theory the record never raises. The criterion rewards knowledge of the rubric, not of the record.

each party shall identify its position --- support, oppose, or no position --- on each of the opposing party's identified motions in limine, to the extent such positions are known at the time of filing.

findings.suggested_fix: Add a record document disclosing Corbin's intended FRE 407 motion, or rewrite C-007 as a general requirement to defend the memo's admissibility.

findings.title: C-008 overstates the trade-usage exception and ignores that express terms prevail over usage
findings.explanation: C-008 requires the answer to concede that trade usage is 'generally admissible' despite an integration clause unless expressly excluded, and to note the EDA does not exclude it. That is incomplete. Under UCC 1-303(e), usage of trade may explain or supplement a contract but cannot override its express terms. Here the express terms are strong: EDA §4.3 makes any MAPC shortfall a material breach, and §8.5 is an anti-waiver clause. Breach liability has also already been decided on summary judgment. Custom evidence that MAPCs are not enforced would contradict those terms. A competent advocate could therefore argue exclusion confidently, citing 1-303(e) and the summary judgment ruling, and still fail C-008 by not making the required concession in a court filing.

evidence.quote: trade usage/industry custom evidence is generally admissible even with an integration clause under UCC § 1-303 or common law unless the contract explicitly excludes trade usage
If Distributor fails to achieve the applicable Minimum Annual Purchase Commitment in any Contract Year, such failure shall constitute a material breach of this Agreement

authorities.proposition: If a consistent construction is unreasonable, express terms prevail over course of performance, course of dealing, and usage of trade.

findings.suggested_fix: Also accept answers that deal with the trade-usage argument by explaining that usage cannot contradict express terms or the summary judgment ruling. Drop the mandatory concession that the motion is weak.

findings.title: Prescott's $4.01M Category 1 rests on an EDA §8.3 quotation that the EDA does not contain; C-032 locks in the figure
findings.explanation: Prescott claims the full MAPC shortfall ($4,010,000) as damages, quoting EDA §8.3: 'any shortfall below the applicable MAPC shall be payable as a direct obligation.' The actual §8.3 is the remediation-plan clause and contains no such language. Holt shows that at the 34% margin the lost profit is $1,363,400. A careful plaintiff's lawyer should correct or flag this before relying on it at trial. C-032's express alternative covers only a lease-based adjustment. Its FAIL clause ('without explanation') may rescue a corrected total, but a judge could read the PASS list as exclusive and fail a more accurate answer. C-033 and C-034 are safe as long as the raw shortfall figures are stated.

findings.title: The limitations criteria tie timeliness to the March 10, 2023 complaint, but testimony says the fraud count was added later by amendment
findings.explanation: C-003 and C-005 treat the March 10, 2023 complaint as the filing that must be timely, and C-005 even accepts 'discovered October 2023' as making the March 2023 filing timely. That is illogical: a fraud discovered in October 2023 cannot have been pleaded in March 2023. Hausman testifies that the original complaint pleaded only breach and that the fraud claim was added by amendment after late-2023 discovery. The pretrial order and summary judgment ruling instead say the original complaint had three counts, and Prescott cites an 'Amended Complaint.' A careful answer might analyze the amendment date and Rule 15(c) relation back, or point to the fall-2022 inquiry-notice date Hausman gives. Such answers could be judged as not matching C-005's specified dates.

findings.title: C-017 accepts an LLC's state of organization and principal office as its citizenship, which is wrong for diversity
findings.explanation: C-017 passes an answer that describes Corbin Supply as a Delaware LLC with principal offices in North Carolina. For diversity purposes, an LLC's citizenship is the citizenship of each of its members, not its state of organization or principal place of business. The criterion therefore rewards a legally wrong analysis, such as an answer calling Corbin 'a citizen of Delaware and North Carolina.' The 'or otherwise identifies complete diversity' language probably saves an answer that analyzes membership correctly, so the practical risk is rewarding error rather than failing correct work.

evidence.quote: PASS if the jurisdictional statement identifies Ridgeline as a Pennsylvania corporation and Corbin Supply as a Delaware LLC with principal offices in North Carolina
The statement shall identify the citizenship of each party

authorities.citation: Zambelli Fireworks Mfg. Co. v. Wood, 592 F.3d 412, 420 (3d Cir. 2010)
authorities.proposition: The citizenship of an LLC for diversity purposes is determined by the citizenship of each of its members.

findings.suggested_fix: Require Corbin's citizenship to be stated through its members (for example, an averment that no member is a Pennsylvania citizen), or at least accept that and not reward the state-of-organization framing alone.

findings.title: C-039 requires a specific 'materiality / law of the case' motion in limine the record does not call for

A competent drafter could reasonably rely on those rulings through stipulated facts and the contested-issues section rather than file a redundant motion. C-039 makes that strategic choice mandatory.

findings.title: Internal record inconsistencies on the remaining contract term and the contract's identity
findings.explanation: Several documents conflict. The summary judgment ruling and Holt describe Years 3–5 as the 'remaining two and a half years,' while Prescott correctly says the remaining term is three years; 2.5 years is only the Allegheny mitigation window. C-046's parenthetical 'rather than 2.5 years (the remainder of the contract term)' repeats that error. The pretrial order calls the contract a 'Master Supply Agreement dated January 15, 2020,' which conflicts with the EDA's March 1, 2021 date that C-042 requires. Prescott's report (May 15, 2024) also responds to Holt's June 2024 positions, and she is quoted at an April 18 deposition saying her report 'was served on May 15.' Misgrading risk is low, but a solver who corrects these points could confuse a judge applying C-046's wording.

blind.overall: The rubric's structural criteria are mostly sound and grounded in the record. These cover caption, judge, trial date, jurisdiction, stipulations, the twelve required sections, witnesses including the Rinaldi omission, exhibits, the damages arithmetic, and the Findlay-memo scienter points. Its fatal defect is that three criteria depend on facts that appear in none of the 11 documents. C-027 and C-008 depend on a defense witness named Gerald Voss, and C-007 on a Corbin FRE 407 motion against the Findlay memo. Under all-pass scoring, even an excellent answer built strictly from the record fails C-027 and C-007, so the task cannot be passed. Secondary issues: C-008's view of trade usage ignores that express terms prevail, and C-017 accepts an incorrect LLC citizenship framing. The limitations criteria conflict with Hausman's testimony that the fraud claim was added by amendment. The rubric also misses, and through C-032 partly locks in, the $4.01M Category 1 figure built on Prescott's misquotation of EDA §8.3.

sol_verdicts.reason: The pretrial order requires the statement to 'identify the citizenship of each party.' C-017 treats Corbin's Delaware formation and Charlotte office as its citizenship. Under Zambelli (3d Cir. 2010), an LLC takes the citizenship of each of its members, and the record gives no member facts. C-017 therefore rewards a legally wrong jurisdictional statement. A correct answer that averts to member citizenship, or flags that the member facts are missing, risks being read as 'omitted.'

The parenthetical is factually wrong. At termination the remaining term (Years 3-5) was about three years; 2.5 years is Allegheny's mitigation window. But Holt's report and the SJ ruling frame the dispute the same way ('the full remaining 2.5 years'). The operative test only asks whether the answer addresses Holt's 12-month argument, which any competent answer does, so misgrading is unlikely. It is a real defect in the record and the wording, but not a confident misgrade.

C-033 and C-034 only check the undisputed shortfall figures ($880K and $3.13M), which the SJ ruling adopts, so neither is a defect. C-032 locks in Prescott's $4.01M Category 1 at full value, and its express alternative covers only a lease correction. Prescott himself gives a margin-adjusted $1,363,400 (Dep. 1011), and the EDA §8.3 he quotes as authority contains no 'direct obligation' language. The FAIL clause's 'without explanation' may save an explained correction, but a judge could read the PASS list as exclusive.

C-005 tracks the plaintiff's position as the SJ ruling records it (early 2023, and October 2023 discovery). But Hausman testifies that concerns arose in fall 2022 and that the fraud count was added by amendment after discovery. The pretrial order says fraud was in the original complaint. An answer that concedes fall-2022 inquiry notice (still timely) or analyzes relation back could fall outside C-005's specified dates. The risk is modest because the FAIL clause targets only answers that give no discovery date.

final.changes_from_blind:
Adopted from Sol:
- C-017 (O3, Sol B6-PT-1): upgraded from arguable to problematic. The court's format expressly requires citizenship, and the criterion both rewards a wrong LLC-citizenship statement and risks failing a correct member-based answer. Zambelli was verified.

Dropped:
- Blind O3 (the C-008 legal error on trade usage). The criterion's 'acknowledges or addresses' standard is lenient enough that an answer arguing express terms prevail under UCC 1-303(e) would pass, so this is ordinary legal judgment. C-008 stays problematic only under O1, as dependent on the nonexistent Voss motion.
- C-003 (from blind O5). Its FAIL condition is triggered only by silence on the limitations defense, so it cannot misgrade.
- C-033 and C-034 (from blind O4). They check the undisputed shortfall figures. My verdict on Sol's B6-PT-3 is mixed for the same reason.
- C-042 and C-035 (from blind O9). Both are consistent with the operative documents.

Refocused:
- Blind O9 now targets C-046 and is merged with Sol B6-PT-2. I kept it at arguable, not Sol's 'confirmed', because Holt and the SJ ruling frame the dispute identically and the operative test only asks whether Holt's argument is addressed.

Retained:
- C-027, C-008, and C-007 stay problematic (O1, O2). Sol did not flag them, but a fresh full-text search again found no Voss, no Gerald, no Rule 407, and no remedial-measures reference in any of the 11 documents.

Unchanged: C-032, C-005, C-039, and C-023 remain arguable.
final.overall: Most of the rubric's structural and arithmetic criteria are grounded in the record: caption, sections, witnesses, exhibits, stipulated figures, and the damages math. Three criteria make the task unwinnable under all-pass scoring. C-027 and C-008 depend on a defense custom witness, Gerald Voss, and C-007 on a Corbin FRE 407 motion against the Findlay memo. Neither appears in any supplied document, so even an excellent answer built from the record fails. Sol missed these, probably because its review was targeted rather than exhaustive. C-017 is also problematic: it equates an LLC's formation state and principal office with diversity citizenship, contrary to Third Circuit law. The remaining findings are arguable. C-032 accepts only a lease-based correction to Prescott's damages total. C-005 fixes discovery dates despite conflicting testimony and pleading history. C-039 demands a materiality motion the record does not call for, C-023 has a gap between its PASS and FAIL conditions, and C-046 carries a record-derived error about the contract term.
